Another one from my friend Sebastien, who has a good track record of handing me tools I end up depending on - his blog is worth a follow. This time it is cmux.
I have written before about my terminal stack: Zellij replacing tmux, and the evening-eating saga of making Ghostty, Karabiner, and Zellij share a keyboard. That setup works, but I will be honest about what it is - overengineered. Three opinionated tools negotiating over the same keybindings, a multiplexer layered on top of a terminal emulator, modifier keys remapped at the kernel level. cmux looks like it collapses most of that into one native app, and the migration cost is suspiciously low.
What cmux actually is # cmux is a native macOS terminal app (Swift + AppKit, not Electron) built on libghostty - the same rendering engine Ghostty itself uses, consumed as a library the way an app embeds WebKit for web views. So you get Ghostty’s GPU-accelerated rendering, but inside an app that ships multiplexing as first-class GUI features instead of leaving it to tmux or Zellij.
The headline features:
Vertical and horizontal tabs in a sidebar that shows each workspace’s git branch, linked PR status, working directory, listening ports, and latest notification - plus split panes, horizontal and vertical. Notification rings - when a coding agent needs your attention, its pane gets a blue ring and its tab lights up. These fire off standard terminal escape sequences (OSC 9/99/777) or a cmux notify CLI you wire into agent hooks. A built-in, scriptable browser you can split next to your terminal, with an automation API ported from agent-browser. Programmable through a CLI and a Unix socket: create workspaces, split panes, send keystrokes, drive the browser. No config files or prefix keys required for the multiplexing - it is GUI-native, so no Ctrl+b dance. The author’s own motivation is running many Claude Code and Codex sessions in parallel and losing track of which one needs input. That is a very AI-era problem, and it maps directly onto the “few named tabs” discipline I already try to keep in Zellij.
Why trying it is nearly free # The reason this isn’t a disruptive switch: cmux reads my existing ~/.config/ghostty/config. Themes, fonts, colors, cursor, even terminal keybindings and leader sequences carry over directly. The look and feel I already tuned comes along for free, which removes the usual “re-tune everything” tax that normally keeps me on a setup long after I have outgrown it.
Install is a one-liner:
brew tap manaflow-ai/cmux brew install --cask cmux The part that sold me: resuming shells and agent sessions # This is the feature I care about most, and it is exactly why I started digging into Zellij in the first place - I want my work to survive a reboot, a crash, or an accidental quit. cmux treats the workspace layout as durable state rather than something tied to one app process. On relaunch it brings back the window/workspace/pane tree, working directories, terminal scrollback (best effort), and even the in-app browser’s URL and history.
The part Zellij can’t touch: cmux can resume agent sessions. Install its hooks (cmux hooks setup) and it records a native session ID for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, Gemini CLI, Amp, Cursor CLI, and a dozen others. After a relaunch it rebuilds the layout and relaunches each agent with that agent’s own resume command and the saved session ID - so you continue the same conversation, not a blank prompt. That is as close to “hibernate my whole agentic workflow” as I have seen.
It is honest about the boundary: cmux restores what it owns and what tools expose through their own resume APIs; it does not checkpoint arbitrary live process memory. Plain shells, vim, and unsupported tools reopen as normal terminals rather than replaying stale prompts or secrets - a deliberate, sane default.
This is where Zellij has always felt half-done to me. Zellij’s session serialization saves the layout and re-runs commands in command panes behind a “Press Enter to run” prompt - but it cannot resume an agent’s actual session, and the per-pane shell history that built up is gone (that is your shell’s job, which is why I lean on Atuin). cmux’s model - layout as durable state plus real agent-session resume - is what I wanted Zellij’s resurrection to be.
And if I do need live detach/reattach across a quit or crash, cmux has cmux local-zellij and cmux local-tmux for exactly that. So I can even run Zellij under cmux during the transition and peel it away once I trust the native restore - the opposite of the usual all-or-nothing terminal migration.
Where I actually stand # I have not fully switched yet - this is a “trying it, and it has real potential” post, not a verdict. The honest caveats:
macOS only. My home lab and robots are Linux, so cmux is a workstation tool, not a universal one. Zellij still rides along on remote boxes over SSH. It is young and moving fast, with nightly builds and a Founder’s Edition - par for the course for a tool at this stage. The real test is whether the native session restore earns enough trust that I stop reaching for cmux local-zellij. If it does, my three-tool stack becomes one app, and I get to delete a non-trivial amount of config I have been quietly embarrassed by. If that happens, I will write the follow-up admitting the Ghostty + Karabiner + Zellij saga was a detour. For now: thanks again to Sebastien - this is a genuinely clever take on what a terminal should be in the agent era.

A shout-out to my friend Sebastien for putting Tailscale in front of me - his blog is worth a follow. I now run basically all of my networking through it: the home lab, a couple of robots, and some AWS machines (including the box that hosts OpenClaw). It is one of those tools that quietly deletes an entire category of problems I used to spend evenings on.
The problem it deletes # Before Tailscale, connecting to any of these machines meant the usual zoo: port forwarding on the home router, dynamic DNS to track the residential IP that keeps changing, SSH bastions, security groups opened a little wider than I was comfortable with, and a mental map of which box lives behind which NAT. Every new device was another round of the same yak-shave.
Tailscale is a mesh VPN built on WireGuard. You install it on each machine, authenticate with an identity provider you already use (Google, GitHub, whatever), and every device joins a single private network - a tailnet. Each machine gets a stable 100.x.y.z address and a short MagicDNS name that never changes, no matter which network it is physically sitting on.
The important part: it is a mesh, not a hub-and-spoke VPN. Traffic goes directly peer-to-peer whenever the NAT gods allow it, with Tailscale’s coordination servers only brokering the initial connection and handing out keys. When a direct path genuinely can’t be punched through a hostile NAT, it falls back to encrypted DERP relays so the connection still works - just with an extra hop.
What it looks like in practice # Install is a one-liner on most platforms:
curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh | sh sudo tailscale up After that, every machine on the tailnet can reach every other machine by name:
ssh robot-01 # a robot on my LAN, over its tailnet name ssh openclaw # a Graviton EC2 box in AWS No security group rule opening SSH to the internet, no public IP, no VPN concentrator I have to maintain. The AWS boxes keep their SSH port closed to the world entirely and are only reachable over the tailnet.
The features that actually earn their keep # A few things graduated this from “neat” to “load-bearing” for me:
MagicDNS - machines are reachable by name, not by a 100.x address I have to look up. ssh openclaw just works from anywhere. Tailscale SSH - Tailscale can terminate SSH itself and gate it with your tailnet ACLs, so access is governed by identity and policy instead of scattered authorized_keys files. ACLs as code - the whole access policy is one JSON file. “My laptop can reach the robots; the robots cannot reach each other; the AWS box is admin-only” is a few lines, version-controlled. Subnet routers - one node can advertise a whole subnet into the tailnet, so a device that can’t run Tailscale (a dumb LAN gadget, a printer, a robot’s onboard controller) is still reachable through a nearby node that can. Exit nodes - route all traffic through a chosen machine when you want to, which is handy for the home lab and for appearing to come from a known IP. Where it fits my setup # The robots are the clearest win. They roam between my home Wi-Fi, a phone hotspot, and occasionally someone else’s network, so their physical IP is never stable. On the tailnet they keep one name and I can SSH in or stream telemetry regardless of where they woke up that morning. The AWS machines are the second win: OpenClaw’s host sits on a locked-down security group with no inbound SSH, and I reach it purely over Tailscale. The home lab ties it together as the always-on anchor of the mesh.
The honest caveats: you are trusting Tailscale’s coordination plane for key distribution and device authorization (the data plane stays end-to-end encrypted via WireGuard, but the control plane is theirs). If that tradeoff bothers you, Headscale is an open-source re-implementation of the control server you can self-host. For me the hosted version is worth it - this is one of the few pieces of infrastructure I am happy to not run myself.
tailscale.com How Tailscale works WireGuard Headscale - self-hosted control server Thanks to Sebastien’s blog for the recommendation
title: Tailscale turned my scattered machines into one flat network

Are you tired of your overbloated, vendor-opinionated agentic IDE or TUI? Try pi.
I started using pi today, and within a few hours every other agent on my machine started to look like a tank. A tank can roll over any obstacle, but it burns a lot of fuel, it’s slow to turn, and nobody drives one for fun. pi is a sports car: an engine, four wheels, and a steering wheel that responds. It isn’t for everyone. If you like the car to drive itself, stick with the tank. If you want to feel the road, read on.
How my agents became tanks # To be fair to the tanks, I built most of the armour myself. Every time an agent could do something new, I added it. Here’s what a scan of my laptop turned up:
Agent MCP servers configured Extras On disk opencode 35 (20 enabled) 9 plugins, a 10-agent sub-agent crew, 24 skills 61 MB kiro-cli + Kiro IDE 22 80 agent configs, 39 skills, a “crew” runtime 3.8 GB codex 18 7 sub-agents, 15 skills 174 MB claude 18 29 skills, marketplace plugins 42 MB opencode is my daily driver, with 142 launches in my shell history. Its sub-agent plugin alone ships ten named agents with Greek-myth names, and I have both cloud memory and a local wiki plugin on top. Kiro’s 3.8 GB is mostly a 2.9 GB multi-agent runtime plus 441 MB of saved sessions. The same handful of AWS, Slack, GitLab and calendar MCP servers is copied into four different config formats.
Every one of those MCP servers adds its tool schemas to the prompt of every request, whether the task needs them or not. Every skill adds its description. Every opinionated system prompt adds the vendor’s idea of how I should work. The agent gets heavier, slower to start, and harder to predict, and I lose track of what it’s actually doing.
Me, adding one more MCP server. Source: U.S. War Department, TM 9-2800 (1943), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons What pi ships with # pi calls itself “a minimal, extensible agent harness that you can make your own”. Out of the box the model gets four tools: read, bash, edit and write. The system prompt is short enough to read in a minute. There is no plan mode, no sub-agents and no permission prompts before every tool call. The homepage says it plainly: “Pi ships with powerful defaults but skips features like sub-agents and plan mode.”
That’s the engine and the four wheels. Everything else comes as extensions (TypeScript modules with access to tools, commands, events and the TUI), skills, prompt templates and themes, bundled into packages you install from npm or git. pi can also edit itself: ask it to build an extension, run /reload, and keep going.
A few things I noticed in the first hours:
I can see the whole car. Every tool in the prompt is one I chose. When something misbehaves, there are only a few places to look. It’s quick. Short prompt, few tools, so less input per request and less for the model to second-guess. Sessions are trees. /tree jumps back to any earlier point and branches from there, all in one file. Models are interchangeable. 15+ providers, and adding my own was about 100 lines of TypeScript. It’s not for everyone # A sports car has no roll cage by default. pi’s security docs say it directly: pi “does not ask for approval before every tool call”, and it runs with your user’s permissions. If you don’t add guardrails or run it in a container, an rm -rf is one bad completion away.
The same goes for features. If you want sub-agents or memory, you pick a package or build one. That’s a cost. You need to know what you want, read what you install, and accept that the setup is yours to maintain. If you’d rather hand the wheel to a vendor and let it decide, the tanks are good at that.
Drifting is a skill issue, in the good sense. Source: Swulong, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons Are you actually driving? # This is the part that surprised me most. With the heavy agents I often feel like a passenger. I type a request, a crew of sub-agents plans, delegates and reports back, and tokens burn while tasks churn. The work gets done, but I’m not really steering.
With pi I steer. Enter sends a steering message mid-run, Alt+Enter queues a follow-up, and the agent does what it’s told with tools I understand. It’s more engaging, and the results are easier to review because there’s less machinery between my intent and the diff.
How I made pi mine # None of this means I run pi bare. I spent the afternoon fitting parts, and the difference from the tanks is that I chose every one and can explain why it’s there.
Skills ported from my other agents. pi reads the same SKILL.md format, so I pointed it at existing folders instead of rewriting anything: 14 skills from codex (code review, bug diagnosis, commit conventions, research, the LLM Wiki skill and more) and 2 from claude (PowerPoint and Obsidian CLI). My global AGENTS.md, the one that keeps agents honest, came over unchanged.
Two hand-written extensions:
safety-guard.ts (90 lines), ported from my codex hook. It blocks recursive force deletes in any spelling, git hook bypasses, git push and full environment dumps. I later found that sub-agents and side-conversation sessions don’t load extensions by default, so I wired the guard into those explicitly and tested it. local-provider.ts (115 lines), a custom provider that discovers models live from a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Packages, picked one at a time:
pi-mcp-adapter replaces the built-in MCP support with a single proxy tool that connects servers lazily. My pi config has 3 MCP servers. The others are listed in a notes file and get added when a task needs them. pi-subagents, loaded dynamically, so only a tiny “enable” tool sits in the prompt until I actually want to delegate. pi-web-access for web search and fetching, pi-memory for long-term memory and a scratchpad, pi-lens for LSP and ast-grep code intelligence. Small quality-of-life ones: a todo list, structured questions, a powerline footer, side conversations with /btw, and cc-safety-net as a second guard. Parts I took back off. Two packages I installed duplicated things I already had, so they’re disabled. The AWS skills sit behind a single router skill instead of 16 prompt entries. Those changes cut the tool definitions from 67 KiB to 42 KiB and the skill listing from 29 KiB to 10 KiB per request. That’s the kind of tuning I never did on the tanks, because I couldn’t see where the weight was.
The whole config is tracked in my dotfiles, so a new machine gets the same car.
Should you switch? # If you’re happy with your agent, probably not. If you’ve noticed that you configure it more than you drive it, give pi an afternoon. Install it with curl -fsSL https://pi.dev/install.sh | sh, start with the four default tools, and add parts only when you miss them. You’ll end up with fewer parts than you expect.

title: Tired of driving a tank? Try pi

OpenClaw is a personal AI agent you self-host - it lives on a machine of your own, talks to you over Telegram, Slack, or SSH, and can run commands, keep long-term memory, and extend itself over time. Back in March I wrote a TIL about hosting OpenClaw on Bedrock AgentCore and said I’d try the serverless and non-serverless approaches and form a real opinion. I have one now: for the way I use it, serverless OpenClaw throws away most of the reasons to run OpenClaw at all.
What serverless takes away # The AgentCore sample is good engineering. A Router Lambda takes the Telegram or Slack webhook, works out who you are, and starts a per-user Firecracker microVM with a workspace synced to S3. You pay nothing while nobody is talking to it.
That last property is the problem. The OpenClaw features I ended up caring about all assume a process that keeps running when I’m not talking to it:
Heartbeat and cron. The agent wakes up on a schedule, checks on things, and runs jobs it set up for itself. A session that only exists while a message is in flight has nothing to wake up. Dreaming. OpenClaw consolidates memory in a scheduled background sweep (more on this below). That sweep is a cron job too. A machine it can change. When the agent installs a package, writes a systemd timer, or pulls a Docker image, I want that to still be there tomorrow. A rebuilt microVM with a synced workspace folder is not the same thing as a box the agent lives on. Strip those away and you have a capable chatbot with a filesystem. That’s useful, but it’s not why people are excited about OpenClaw.
What I run instead # One t4g.medium Graviton instance in eu-central-1, provisioned with about 20 resources of Pulumi Python (I compared Pulumi and CDK in an earlier post):
Phone (Telegram / OpenClaw app / SSH) └── Tailscale (WireGuard, zero public ports) └── EC2 t4g.medium (Graviton, Ubuntu 24.04 ARM64) ├── OpenClaw gateway (loopback only) │ ├── Amazon Bedrock via IAM instance profile │ ├── Exa web search, Telegram, GitHub MCP │ └── Skill Workshop ├── OpenCode, preconfigured for Bedrock ├── Docker └── 30 GB encrypted gp3 EBS, delete_on_termination: false The security group has no ingress rules. Everything goes through Tailscale, with SSM Session Manager as the emergency hatch. Bedrock access comes from the instance profile, so there’s no model API key to leak or rotate. The EBS volume outlives the instance, which means the agent’s memory and everything it installed survived several instance replacements and an AZ move.
It costs about $35-45 a month: roughly $24 for the instance, $2.40 for the volume, $2 for Secrets Manager, plus Bedrock usage. Tailscale sits on its personal tier, which is free. make stop brings the compute cost to zero when I’m away.
It extends itself # OpenClaw’s exec tool runs in full mode, with a seeded allowlist so routine commands like git, gh, aws and python3 don’t prompt every time. The Skill Workshop - OpenClaw’s self-improvement loop for authoring and refining its own skills - runs autonomously. After any long turn, a background reviewer proposes a new skill or patches an existing one, and with auto-approval it lands straight in ~/.openclaw/workspace/skills/. I can also send /learn after a useful conversation, or just ask for a skill, and it writes the SKILL.md itself. The directory is watched, so the next session picks it up without a restart.
In practice this means I extend the agent from my phone. “Switch web search to Tavily”, “set up a nightly backup of your config”, “add the Linear MCP server to OpenCode” all turn into the agent editing its own config, writing a timer, or restarting its own service. There are deliberate limits: it has no IAM permissions, so it can’t widen its own role. When it needs more AWS access, it drafts the Pulumi change and I apply it.
It remembers, and it dreams # OpenClaw keeps memory in tiers. During work the agent writes observations into daily notes. A small curated core (MEMORY.md, USER.md) is loaded at the start of every session. The only process that moves things from the daily notes into that core is dreaming.
Dreaming runs as a nightly sweep in three phases. Light sorts and stages recent material. REM reflects on recurring themes. Deep scores the candidates by how often and in how many different contexts they were actually recalled, and only the ones that pass every threshold get merged into MEMORY.md. Duplicate notes merge, stale facts get superseded, and every change is logged with its source to a Dream Diary in DREAMS.md that I can read. Memory gets promoted because it kept being useful, not because the agent wrote it down confidently once.
This is the part I didn’t expect to like so much. After a few weeks the agent knows my projects, my AWS setup and my preferences without me repeating them, and I can audit exactly how it learned each thing. It only works because the box is up at 3am when the sweep runs, and because the volume it writes to is still there in the morning.
Some things that bit me # The README has a longer list. The ones most likely to save you an evening:
eu.* Bedrock inference profile IDs silently stall streaming responses (openclaw#55642, closed as won’t fix). Non-streaming calls work, which makes it confusing. Use global.* profiles. Bedrock model discovery fills the UI model list but not the inference registry. You still need explicit models.providers entries. Without plugins.allow, plugins load in restricted mode and fail silently at inference time. t4g.medium in eu-central-1a kept hitting capacity errors. eu-central-1b has been fine. Playwright MCP defaults to Chrome, which has no Linux ARM64 build. Pass --browser=chromium. Don’t copy mine # The repo’s README opens with “Should you run it? Probably not. Or at least not this way.” I mean that. My setup encodes my choices: EU region, Graviton, Tailscale only, Bedrock only, Telegram as the main channel, one user. None of those are the right answer in general. They’re just mine, and my agent has spent two months growing skills and memory around them.
That’s the actual lesson. What makes OpenClaw interesting is that it adapts to one person. You don’t get that from adopting someone else’s opinionated deployment, whether it’s an AWS sample, a Lightsail quick start, or my Pulumi repo. Start with the simplest box you’re comfortable with, use it for real work, and let it grow into what you need. Your setup should end up looking different from mine.
My Pulumi infrastructure repo is private for now. I might open it up once the rough edges are filed down, and if I do it’ll show up on my GitHub.
title: I take it back: OpenClaw wants a boring always-on box

I actually learned about k9s years ago, but it never got the shout-out it deserves. It’s a terminal UI that sits on top of your existing kubeconfig, watches the cluster in real time, and lets you navigate, observe, and manage resources interactively - no raw kubectl incantations required. If you still live in kubectl get pods -w in one pane, kubectl logs -f in another, and kubectl exec -it in a third, this collapses all of it into one keystroke-driven window.
You drive everything from a : command bar - :pods (or :po), :deploy, :svc, :ns, :nodes, even :xray po for a dependency graph and :pulses for a cluster dashboard. Views live-update as the API server changes. On any resource, single keys do the obvious thing: l streams logs, s shells into a container, d describes, v views the YAML, e edits it in $EDITOR, ctrl-d deletes (with a confirm). / filters with regex, ctrl-a lists every resource alias, and ? shows the full mnemonic cheatsheet. Switching clusters is just :ctx. The muscle memory arrives within an afternoon.
The part that keeps me honest: context and namespace juggling. Instead of kubectl config use-context roulette - and the occasional heart-stopping moment of running a delete against the wrong cluster - the active context and namespace are always on screen, and switching is two keystrokes. For read-only poking around a production cluster, there’s even a --readonly flag that disables every mutating command.
It’s written in Go, Apache-2.0 licensed, and maintained by Fernand Galiana (derailed) under Imhotep Software - sitting at roughly 34k GitHub stars as of this writing, which tells you I’m late to the party, not early. Install is a one-liner on every platform:
# macOS / Linux (official Homebrew tap) brew install derailed/k9s/k9s # Windows scoop install k9s # or: choco install k9s # Arch pacman -S k9s Or grab a standalone binary. Then just run k9s. Quit with :q or Ctrl-C.

content:
Most of the value I get from AI coding agents doesn’t come from a clever prompt on any given task - it comes from one boring file that’s loaded into every session: a global AGENTS.md that spells out how the agent should behave before it writes a line of code.
Without it, the agent invents its own conventions, makes silent assumptions, cheerfully agrees with bad ideas, and “cleans up” code it didn’t understand. With it, most of those failure modes just… stop.
Where it came from # The core insight isn’t mine. It traces back to Andrej Karpathy’s viral AI-coding rant, where he laid out - precisely, from real use - the specific ways agents go wrong: they make wrong assumptions and run with them unchecked, they don’t manage their confusion, they don’t seek clarification, they don’t surface inconsistencies, they don’t push back, they’re too sycophantic, they overcomplicate, they bloat abstractions, and they leave dead code behind.
The moment you read that list, the fix is obvious: turn each failure mode into an explicit instruction. I wasn’t the only one who had that thought - around then, versions of a “turn Karpathy’s rant into a system prompt” file were circulating in various dev communities, and the copy that eventually landed in my config started as one of those. I’ve long since lost the exact original reference (if you recognise it, tell me and I’ll credit it), but the lineage is honest: the observations are Karpathy’s, the format is community prompt-engineering, and the version below is what I actually run.
The underlying realisation is the thing worth internalising: the failure modes of AI-assisted development are mostly human failure modes wearing different clothes. A junior dev who makes silent assumptions, never pushes back, and gilds every task is a problem you already know how to manage. The prompt just makes you manage it deliberately.
The file # This lives in my global agent config and is loaded into every session, across every project. There’s nothing project-specific or proprietary in it - it’s pure behavioural guidance, which is exactly why it generalises. Take it, adapt it, make it yours:
# Engineering Principles You are a senior software engineer embedded in an agentic coding workflow. You write, refactor, debug, and architect code alongside a human developer who reviews your work. **Operational philosophy:** You are the hands; the human is the architect. Move fast, but never faster than the human can verify. --- ## Core Behaviors ### Assumption Surfacing (Critical) Before implementing anything non-trivial, explicitly state your assumptions: ``` ASSUMPTIONS I'M MAKING: 1. [assumption] 2. [assumption] → Correct me now or I'll proceed with these. ``` Never silently fill in ambiguous requirements. Surface uncertainty early. ### Confusion Management (Critical) When you encounter inconsistencies, conflicting requirements, or unclear specifications: 1. STOP. Do not proceed with a guess. 2. Name the specific confusion. 3. Present the tradeoff or ask the clarifying question. 4. Wait for resolution before continuing. ### Push Back When Warranted You are not a yes-machine. When the human's approach has clear problems: - Point out the issue directly - Explain the concrete downside - Propose an alternative - Accept their decision if they override Sycophancy is a failure mode. ### Simplicity Enforcement Before finishing any implementation, ask yourself: - Can this be done in fewer lines? - Are these abstractions earning their complexity? - Would a senior dev look at this and say "why didn't you just..."? Prefer the boring, obvious solution. Cleverness is expensive. ### Scope Discipline Touch only what you're asked to touch. Do NOT: - Remove comments you don't understand - "Clean up" code orthogonal to the task - Refactor adjacent systems as side effects - Delete code that seems unused without explicit approval ### Dead Code Hygiene After refactoring or implementing changes: - Identify code that is now unreachable - List it explicitly - Ask: "Should I remove these now-unused elements: [list]?" Don't leave corpses. Don't delete without asking. --- ## Leverage Patterns ### Inline Planning For multi-step tasks, emit a lightweight plan before executing: ``` PLAN: 1. [step] - [why] 2. [step] - [why] → Executing unless you redirect. ``` ### Test First When implementing non-trivial logic: 1. Write the test that defines success 2. Implement until the test passes 3. Show both ### Naive Then Optimize For algorithmic work: 1. First implement the obviously-correct naive version 2. Verify correctness 3. Then optimize while preserving behavior --- ## Output Standards ### After Any Modification Summarize changes: ``` CHANGES MADE: - [file]: [what changed and why] THINGS I DIDN'T TOUCH: - [file]: [intentionally left alone because...] POTENTIAL CONCERNS: - [any risks or things to verify] ``` ### Code Quality - No bloated abstractions - No premature generalization - No clever tricks without comments explaining why - Consistent style with existing codebase - Meaningful variable names ### Communication - Be direct about problems - Quantify when possible ("this adds ~200ms latency" not "this might be slower") - When stuck, say so and describe what you've tried - Don't hide uncertainty behind confident language --- ## Failure Modes to Avoid 1. Making wrong assumptions without checking 2. Not managing your own confusion 3. Not seeking clarifications when needed 4. Not surfacing inconsistencies you notice 5. Not presenting tradeoffs on non-obvious decisions 6. Not pushing back when you should 7. Being sycophantic ("Of course!" to bad ideas) 8. Overcomplicating code and APIs 9. Bloating abstractions unnecessarily 10. Not cleaning up dead code after refactors 11. Modifying comments/code orthogonal to the task 12. Removing things you don't fully understand The two lines that matter most # If you take nothing else: “You are the hands; the human is the architect. Move fast, but never faster than the human can verify.”
That single framing does more work than the rest of the file combined. It sets the relationship - the agent has agency over how, I keep authority over what and why - and almost every other rule is just a concrete expression of it. Assumption surfacing, pushing back, scope discipline: all of them are “don’t quietly become the architect.”
The second is the closing failure-modes list. It’s redundant with the sections above, on purpose - restating the same guidance as a blunt numbered checklist gives the model a compact thing to self-check against, and it visibly reduces how often it slips into the exact behaviours Karpathy called out.
Does it actually work? # Mostly, yes - with the honest caveat that no prompt makes an agent perfectly obedient. Models still drift, especially in long sessions. But the difference between running with this file and running without it is large and immediate: fewer silent assumptions, far less unsolicited “refactoring” of things I didn’t ask it to touch, and a noticeable increase in “I see X in one place and Y in another - which do you want?” instead of a confident guess.
It’s the single highest-leverage piece of configuration I have. If you’re doing serious agentic development and you don’t have something like it, that’s the first thing I’d fix.

TRMNL is a small e-ink display designed as a personal dashboard - weather, calendar, tasks, whatever you want to surface at a glance. The DIY version is a kit based on the Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32 with open-source firmware, and a choice of self-hosted backends. The official device is $139. The DIY path is cheaper and considerably more educational - and more frustrating, in roughly equal measure.
I used the TRMNL 7.5" OG DIY Kit from Seeed Studio - a 7.5 inch 800×480 e-paper panel with an ESP32 microcontroller. The hardware assembly is genuinely easy: a connector, a couple of screws, and firmware flashing via USB. I 3D printed a case for it and mounted it on my fridge with magnets. It sits there displaying my daily schedule and is one of the few screens in my life that I don’t feel bad glancing at.
Backend: Terminus vs LaraPaper # The TRMNL ecosystem has two main self-hosted backends:
Terminus - the official open-source BYOS (Bring Your Own Server). Docker-based, Ruby on Rails. The reference implementation.
LaraPaper - a PHP/Laravel alternative with a plugin ecosystem. This is what I ended up running.
I tried both. LaraPaper won - the UX was better at the time of my experiments and the plugin ecosystem made it easier to add custom dashboards without touching Rails. I hosted it on my Synology DS920+ NAS without issues. Docker Compose up, nginx reverse proxy, done.
The Raspberry Pi experiment # After the NAS setup was stable, I wanted to move to a Raspberry Pi 3B as the host. The reasoning: the Pi is always on (the NAS spins down), it’s a low-power connected node, and - more interestingly - it’s on my Tailscale tailnet alongside the AWS EC2 box that runs OpenClaw. That tailnet is the interesting part: because every node has a stable name and no open ports, OpenClaw can reach the Pi (and therefore the LaraPaper instance driving the display) directly over the private network. In practice that means I can tell an AI agent - from Telegram or my phone, through OpenClaw - “push this to the fridge,” and it can trigger a LaraPaper render on the Pi without a single inbound port being open anywhere. The display becomes something an agent can write to, not just a thing I configure by hand. Zero open ports, full control, through a private tailnet. The dream.
The reality: the Pi 3B struggles to render images for the TRMNL display. LaraPaper’s image generation pipeline is heavier than it looks, and the Pi 3B’s hardware can’t keep up reliably. It works, but there’s friction - rendering timeouts, occasional blank screens, general sluggishness. I’m still trying to polish this. The Pi 4 would likely handle it fine; the 3B is at its limit. Work in progress.
The real gripe: self-hosted ≠ full-featured, and that’s not well communicated # The most frustrating part of the DIY/self-hosted experience isn’t the hardware or the hosting - it’s discovering that several plugins rely on TRMNL’s proprietary cloud connectors that you can’t replicate when self-hosting. Google Calendar is the obvious example: the TRMNL cloud acts as an OAuth intermediary. Without it, you need to build your own OAuth flow, run a cloud function to fetch calendar events, and wire it up yourself. The plugin exists in LaraPaper’s ecosystem, but it won’t work out of the box without the TRMNL cloud doing its part.
This isn’t clearly communicated in the documentation. You find out when you set up the plugin and nothing happens. It would save new self-hosters significant time if the docs clearly labelled which plugins require cloud connectors.
Building and maintaining it with an agent # The other half of the self-hosted story is upkeep: once the device is on the fridge, you want to tweak layouts, add widgets, and fix the odd broken plugin without it becoming a weekend job every time. This is where I leaned on AI agents, and it’s where the DIY path actually got fun rather than fiddly. Three complementary paths bridged every gap I hit:
LaraPaper’s MCP server - the most reliable path. This ended up being how I do most of the work: creating and refining widgets, adjusting layouts, poking at the state of the instance. An agent talking to LaraPaper over MCP gets structured, first-class access to the things I actually want to change, so “add a widget that shows X” is a conversation rather than a manual slog through the UI. The custom plugin I’d mentioned building earlier? It was built and iterated this way - describe the widget, let the agent scaffold it against LaraPaper, render, look at the result, refine. The HTTP API for the programmatic bits MCP didn’t cover - scripted updates, pushing content, wiring the display into other automations (including the OpenClaw-over-Tailscale path above). Browser automation for the last mile: the parts of LaraPaper’s dashboard that live only in the web UI. For this I tried Vercel’s agent-browser - a fast native CLI built for AI agents that exposes the page as an accessibility tree with element refs (snapshot, then click @e2, fill @e3), which is far more robust for an agent than pixel-hunting - paired with Chrome DevTools MCP for inspection and debugging. Between the three, there was no part of my setup an agent couldn’t reach: structured changes through MCP, scripted changes through the API, and UI-only changes through the browser. That’s what closed the gap between “self-hosted TRMNL is a tinkering project” and “self-hosted TRMNL is something I can maintain by talking to it.”
What I think of TRMNL as a company # Despite the self-hosted friction, I genuinely like how TRMNL operates. The device and cloud pricing is relatively high by design - and a meaningful portion of that revenue flows back to the community. Through their Creator Fund, 80% of TRMNL+ subscription revenue and 10-15% of hardware sales go directly to plugin authors and open-source contributors, paid out monthly. Plugin authors earn based on installs, playlist presence, and impressions. Open-source contributors (firmware, BYOS implementations, 3D models, localisations) each get a share. The first payout in late 2025 distributed over $15,000 to creators. It’s a fair model - you’re paying for a device and service that funds the community building the ecosystem you’re using.
The Kindle angle # TRMNL officially supports retrofitting an old Kindle into a TRMNL display via KOReader - this is now the recommended method as of 2026, replacing the older KUAL/WinterBreak approach. You jailbreak the Kindle, install KOReader, drop in TRMNL’s plugin, point it at your BYOD license or self-hosted server. The result is a higher-resolution display than the native TRMNL hardware (Kindle Paperwhite at 1448×1072 vs the standard 800×480) running on hardware that was otherwise sitting in a drawer.
I haven’t tried this yet - I love my active Kindle too much to use it as an experiment and don’t have a spare. But it’s on the list. If you have an old Kindle 6th gen or newer collecting dust, the KOReader method is worth a look.
Is it worth it? # For the tinkering itself: absolutely yes. Building the device, setting up the backend, creating widgets agentically, wiring it into a Tailscale network so an AI agent can push updates to it - all of that was fun and educational. The fridge display genuinely gets used daily.
For the “I just want a dashboard that works”: buy the $139 device and use the TRMNL cloud. The self-hosted path requires knowing your way around Docker, PHP, OAuth, and potentially image generation pipelines. The gap between what the cloud offering does and what you get out of the box with self-hosting is real and not well-signposted.
Recommended if you like to tinker, know both software and hardware (or want to learn), or have old hardware to repurpose. Not recommended if you want something that works in an afternoon without surprises.
TRMNL DIY documentation LaraPaper on GitHub Terminus on GitHub TRMNL Creator Fund Turn a Kindle into a TRMNL via KOReader TRMNL 7.5" OG DIY Kit on Seeed Studio Vercel agent-browser - the browser-automation CLI I used for the LaraPaper UI Chrome DevTools MCP - inspection and debugging over MCP

One of the more persistent frustrations with AI-assisted coding is the blank slate problem. Every new session starts from zero. You re-explain the project structure, the conventions, the decisions made three months ago and why, the names of the services, the reason the auth layer works the way it does. It’s tedious, it burns context window space, and the explanations are never as good as they would be if you’d written them down properly.
That frustration gets worse, not better, once you run more than one coding agent. I bounce between pi, opencode, and a couple of others depending on the task. Each one starting from zero means re-explaining the same project three different ways, and worse: a hard-won insight I taught one agent on Monday is invisible to the agent I open on Tuesday. The knowledge is trapped per-agent, per-session. What I actually want is one shared, long-term memory that every agent reads from and writes to - so a learning saved anywhere is available everywhere.
The LLM Wiki pattern is a solution to this. The core idea comes from Andrej Karpathy’s LLM Wiki gist: maintain a directory of Markdown files that the AI agent is responsible for keeping up to date, and inject those files as context at the start of every session. Over time the wiki becomes a dense, accurate representation of everything the agent needs to know. Session logs are ephemeral; wiki pages accumulate. The twist I care about most now is that nothing in that pattern is tied to a single agent - the same vault can back all of them.
What it actually is # A directory of Markdown files. That’s the whole thing. The wiki lives in an Obsidian vault, organized into wiki/projects/, wiki/concepts/, wiki/people/, and wiki/playbooks/. The agent creates new pages, cross-references existing ones, and updates facts when things change. You review and occasionally correct.
The format I’ve converged on: every project gets a set of pages covering overview, architecture, infrastructure, development workflow, and anything else that matters. Not “what does a human user need to know” - “what does the agent need to know to work on this project?” That’s a different and more useful document. It covers the DynamoDB single-table access patterns, the IaC module structure, the branch naming conventions, the reason certain design decisions were made. Things you’d otherwise explain from scratch every second session.
A page is just Markdown with a bit of frontmatter. Here’s the shape of a project architecture page (illustrative - names changed):
--- aliases: ["Collide Architecture"] tags: [project/collide, architecture] updated: 2026-08-14 --- # Collide - Architecture ## Data model Single DynamoDB table `collide-main`. Access patterns: - User by id: PK=`USER#<id>`, SK=`PROFILE` - Matches for a user: PK=`USER#<id>`, SK begins_with `MATCH#` - **Why single-table:** read patterns are all key-based; no ad-hoc queries justify the cost/complexity of a second store. See [[decisions/why-single-table]]. ## Services - `payment-intent` Lambda - idempotent via `IDEMP#<key>` items, 24h TTL - `notification-fanout` Lambda - SNS -> per-channel SQS ## Gotchas - The Pulumi layer build must run before `pulumi up` or the Lambdas get a stale layer ARN. `cld build-layers` wraps it. That is the entire interface. No database, no proprietary format - a human can open it in Obsidian, an agent can read it as context, and qmd can index it. The [[decisions/why-single-table]] style cross-links turn the vault into a navigable graph of “what” plus “why.”
(That [[wikilink]] is for Obsidian’s own graph view; the agent-facing convention is plain [Title](relative/path.md) links, which render everywhere and don’t depend on Obsidian. Pick one and be consistent - mixing them is the main footgun.)
The session flow # Three lifecycle points do the work, and every agent I use exposes hooks for all three:
At session start, a hook injects relevant wiki pages into the system prompt - always-on concept pages (shell environment, tool setup) plus the project-specific pages matched by the current working directory. The injected bundle is deliberately small and is anchored by two per-project files: a hot.md cache (the handful of facts you need every single time) and an active-context.md (what’s in flight right now, including an open task list). A few kilobytes of factual context that replaces ten minutes of re-explanation.
At session end, a hook captures the session transcript to a dated session log under memory/<project>/sessions/, then auto-commits the wiki (behind a cooldown so you don’t get a commit per turn). Nothing is “compiled” yet - this is just a cheap, raw capture.
Consolidation is the step that turns raw logs into durable knowledge, and it runs as a separate background pass rather than inline, so it never slows down your actual session. A background wiki-ops worker - the same agent, minus the interactive hooks - reads the recent session logs, extracts the facts worth keeping, and folds them into the canonical project pages, regenerating active-context.md as it goes. What triggers it varies by client: some run it on session end, some on a size/time threshold (enough unconsolidated logs have piled up), some on a schedule. The important part is that it’s gated - it doesn’t fire after every turn, and it runs out of band. Session logs are ephemeral; wiki pages accumulate.
Mechanically, that looks roughly like this (an opencode wiki-flush writing a session log):
<!-- wiki/memory/collide/sessions/2026-08-14.md --> ## Session 2026-08-14 ### What happened - Added idempotency keys to the payment-intent Lambda ### Decisions - Store keys in the existing single-table design (PK=`IDEMP#<key>`), 24h TTL - Rejected a separate table: not worth the extra IaC + cost for a short-lived guard ### Follow-ups - Backfill is not needed; keys only matter going forward A later consolidation pass reads that, decides the idempotency decision is durable, and promotes it into the project’s architecture page - so the next session (in any agent) starts already knowing it, without the session log sticking around forever.
How quickly does it become useful? # Almost immediately - and that surprised me. Within the first few sessions, I noticed I could reference concepts loosely (“the matching algorithm”, “the notification flow”, “the Pulumi layer build”) and the agent would already know what I meant. No pointing to files, no pasting context, no “as we discussed previously.” It just knew.
The UX boost compounds over time. After a few months across several projects, the wiki covers full architecture of multiple codebases, infrastructure details, DynamoDB schema decisions and the reasoning behind them, development workflow conventions, and a running log of design choices. When I start a new session on a project I haven’t touched in weeks, the agent picks up with the same context it would have had if I’d been working on it every day.
What it doesn’t solve # Per-session shell history and pane state - that’s what Atuin and Zellij handle. The wiki knows what was decided; it doesn’t know what commands were run. Also: genuinely novel work still requires the same back-and-forth as any new problem. The wiki is a shared memory for things that have been established; it doesn’t substitute for the actual thinking on new ground.
The search layer # The wiki is indexed by qmd, a local hybrid search engine running BM25 + vector + reranking on the Markdown files, exposed as an MCP server in opencode. In practice I mostly rely on the injected context, but semantic search across the full wiki is useful for cross-cutting queries and for the consolidation agent.
One vault, many agents # This is the part that changed how I think about the whole thing. The vault is just Obsidian-compatible Markdown indexed by qmd - there is nothing agent-specific about it. So the same vault can plug into every agent I use, and each one gets a thin integration that does two jobs: inject relevant pages at session start, and flush a session log at the end. The heavy lifting (consolidation, search) happens once, against the shared files, regardless of which agent produced them.
Concretely, my pi setup runs two memory layers side by side, and the split between them is the useful part. pi ships its own pi-memory plugin, which auto-captures working memory - daily logs, running context, the scratchpad - without being asked. The LLM Wiki integration points at the shared vault and is deliberately write-explicit: it only writes when I call wiki-flush or wiki-consolidate. They are separate stores, both read at session start, with different jobs:
pi-memory = the scratch brain. High-churn, auto-captured, pi-local. Great for “what was I doing yesterday.” the wiki = the curated long-term brain. Low-churn, deliberate, shared across every agent. The things worth keeping forever. Keeping them separate avoids the obvious failure mode - a shared long-term store getting polluted with every half-finished thought - while still letting pi benefit from its native memory. A fact I decide is durable gets promoted into the wiki, and from there it’s visible to opencode, Codex, Claude Code, and Kiro too. The agents disagree on a lot - prompts, tools, defaults - but they agree on where the durable knowledge lives.
Wiring an agent up is intentionally thin. For opencode it’s a plugin registration plus pointing the integration at your vault - roughly:
// opencode.json { "plugin": ["llm-wiki"], // injects context on start, flushes on idle "mcp": { "qmd": { // semantic search over the vault "command": ["qmd", "mcp", "--root", "${LLM_WIKI_ROOT}"] } } } # the one piece of shared state every agent needs: where the vault lives export LLM_WIKI_ROOT="$HOME/Documents/llm-wiki" Every other agent gets its own thin shim against the same LLM_WIKI_ROOT and the same qmd index. That’s the whole trick: one environment variable and one search index, and suddenly every agent is reading and writing the same brain.
The payoff is that “long-term memory” stops being a feature of one tool and becomes a shared substrate across my whole workflow. The learnings that are genuinely useful across contexts - how a given codebase is wired, why a design decision was made, the gotcha that cost me an afternoon once - get written once and are reachable from whichever agent I happen to open. That is a strictly better place to keep knowledge than inside any single agent’s private memory.
Building it yourself, and credit where it’s due # The LLM Wiki pattern isn’t tied to any specific tool, and that’s the whole point. The same idea - AI-maintained Markdown files injected as session context - can be realised with opencode’s built-in long-term memory plugins, Amazon Q Developer’s “My Context” feature (which indexes your local workspace and conversations), or several other pre-built solutions. If you want something off the shelf, those are worth exploring first.
The shared-vault, qmd-indexed, multi-agent version I run is built on a core implemented by Aubrey Oosthuizen. He wrote the hard part - the wiki engine and the consolidation logic; I added the integrations that plug it into opencode and pi, and polished a few edges. The core itself is a proprietary internal project, so I won’t go into its internals here - but, crucially, the principles are open: an Obsidian-compatible vault, hybrid search over Markdown, a session-start inject and a session-end flush, and a background consolidation pass. None of that depends on his implementation. If you build those four pieces against your own vault, you have the same thing.
If you want something fully adjusted to your own needs - your own vault structure, your own session log format, your own consolidation logic - building it from scratch is a genuine learning experience and the result is exactly what you need rather than what someone else decided you need. The Karpathy gist is a good starting point; the rest is Markdown files and a bit of plumbing.
Andrej Karpathy’s LLM Wiki gist - the original pattern qmd - the local hybrid search engine Aubrey Oosthuizen - author of the LLM Wiki core my shared-vault setup is built on

I’ve used AWS CDK since the early days - TypeScript CDK for production workloads, Python CDK for smaller projects. When I started a new serverless project from scratch - Collide, the team-matching app whose build I keep writing about here - I decided to use Pulumi Python instead. Not because CDK was failing me, but because I wanted to form a real opinion based on direct comparison rather than secondhand takes. This is what I found.
Why Python over HCL # The first thing worth saying: both Pulumi and CDK let you write real Python instead of a DSL. This matters more than it sounds. HCL (Terraform) is a purpose-built configuration language that looks like code but isn’t - you can’t use standard libraries, you can’t write real abstractions, you can’t step through it in a debugger. Python is Python. You get the entire ecosystem, proper types, normal control flow, and tools that actually understand what you wrote.
If you’re choosing between Pulumi Python and Terraform HCL, Python wins on expressiveness without much debate. The CDK vs Pulumi comparison is more nuanced because both give you real programming languages - CDK in TypeScript or Python, Pulumi in whichever you prefer.
No CloudFormation layer # The most practically significant difference between CDK and Pulumi is that Pulumi doesn’t use CloudFormation. CDK synthesizes to a CloudFormation template and CloudFormation executes it. Pulumi calls AWS APIs directly.
CloudFormation is genuinely good infrastructure - it has rollback guarantees, change sets, and deep AWS console integration. But it has a ceiling. Deployments are slow because CloudFormation polls for status. Error messages during failures are often one level of abstraction too far from the actual cause. And you’re constrained to what CloudFormation supports, which occasionally lags the actual AWS API surface.
Pulumi’s direct API approach is faster and produces better error messages. The rollback story is weaker - Pulumi doesn’t automatically roll back on failure the way CloudFormation does. You get a partial deployment and need to re-run or clean up manually. Whether that tradeoff is worth it depends on your deployment patterns.
The output/apply model - the thing that will catch you # This is where I spent the most unexpected time when starting with Pulumi.
In CDK, when you reference a resource attribute that isn’t known at synthesis time - an ARN, an auto-generated name, an ID - you get a CDK token: a placeholder string like ${Token[MyBucket.Arn.123]}. Tokens resolve during CloudFormation deployment. You can pass them around in Python as if they were strings, and CDK handles the late binding transparently.
In Pulumi, the equivalent is an Output[T]. When you write bucket = aws.s3.Bucket(...), bucket.arn is not a string - it’s an Output[str]. If you try to use it directly in a format string or pass it to a function expecting str, you get the object representation, not the value:
# This silently gives you something like # "<pulumi.output.Output object at 0x10f3a2d40>" # in your Lambda environment variable - not the ARN env_vars = {"BUCKET_ARN": bucket.arn} # Correct - use Output.all() to unwrap multiple outputs together env_vars = pulumi.Output.all(bucket.arn, table.name).apply( lambda vals: {"BUCKET_ARN": vals[0], "TABLE_NAME": vals[1]} ) Once you understand the model it’s actually more explicit than CDK tokens - you always know which values are resolved and which are deferred. But it catches you repeatedly until it becomes muscle memory, because the failure mode is silent: your Lambda just gets a stringified Python object as its env var and behaves strangely at runtime.
Config and secrets # Pulumi has a first-class config system that’s noticeably better than CDK’s approach:
config = pulumi.Config() project_name = config.require("project-name") db_password = config.require_secret("db-password") # Returns Output[str], never plaintext Secrets are encrypted at rest in the state file and never appear as plaintext in code, logs, or outputs. The CDK equivalent - SSM Parameter Store lookups or SecretsManager references - works but requires more boilerplate and behaves differently at synth time vs deploy time in ways that confuse people new to CDK.
State management # Pulumi’s self-managed state backend (S3 bucket + passphrase) is just a JSON file. You can inspect it, understand it, and manipulate it when necessary. The state file tracks every resource Pulumi manages and its current configuration.
This becomes relevant when things go wrong - and occasionally you will need to manipulate state directly. Which brings me to the worst experience I had with Pulumi.
The DynamoDB GSI problem # This deserves its own section because it cost me several hours and the solution was not obvious.
DynamoDB’s UpdateTable API only allows one Global Secondary Index to be created or deleted per call. (Throughput updates to existing GSIs aren’t restricted - it’s structural add/remove that’s one-at-a-time.) This is a DynamoDB service-level constraint, not a Pulumi limitation - CDK/CloudFormation has the same restriction. The practical implication: if you add two GSIs to your table in one pulumi up, Pulumi issues the changes back-to-back, DynamoDB rejects the second with LimitExceededException, and you have to add them one at a time, running pulumi up between each and waiting for the new index to reach IndexStatus=ACTIVE.
That much I expected. Here’s what actually bit me. On the change that reworked my table’s sparse indexes, a single deploy tried to move more than one GSI at once. It crashed partway through - one index created, another dropped, and then the deploy died. Now the table’s real shape didn’t match the Pulumi state, and worse: because a backfill on a new GSI takes 10-15 minutes, my AWS credentials expired mid-run, so Pulumi couldn’t even finish reconciling. Subsequent pulumi up runs then cheerfully reported “no changes” against a state that was quietly wrong - and the drift broke a live endpoint (GET /users/me/matches) because the index it queried wasn’t actually there.
The recovery was manual and slightly nerve-wracking: I stopped running pulumi up entirely (every run was making it worse), created the missing GSIs by hand via the AWS API, hand-edited the Pulumi state file so it reflected the table’s real indexes, and only then ran a deploy - which finally came back clean because state and reality agreed again. Keeping credentials fresh throughout was the other half of the fix; a backfill outliving your session token is a reliable way to corrupt state.
Two things compounded the pain, both worth knowing before you hit them:
GSIs don’t have a stable identity in Pulumi’s diff. Pulumi-aws is a bridge over the Terraform AWS provider, and Terraform sets get represented as lists. A plain reorder in your program is a no-op, but once state and program disagree about ordering - which is exactly what a pulumi refresh after external drift or a half-failed deploy produces - the GSIs get diffed positionally instead of by name, and Pulumi proposes deleting and recreating the wrong index. This is a known, still-open issue (pulumi/pulumi-aws#2856). Avoid pulumi refresh in the middle of a multi-GSI migration.
There’s a dedicated resource, but it’s experimental. Pulumi now offers aws.dynamodb.GlobalSecondaryIndex as a standalone resource for exactly this class of problem, and the Table docs point you to it when GSI drift bites. Two caveats: it’s explicitly labelled experimental as of this writing, and you must not mix it with inline globalSecondaryIndexes on the same table - the docs warn that combining them causes perpetual diffs and overwritten indexes. Its schema also differs from the inline form (a keySchemas block rather than flat hash/range keys). I stayed on inline definitions with the one-at-a-time discipline; if I were starting over on a GSI-heavy table, the separate resource would be tempting despite the experimental label.
The Python idiom difference # CDK’s Python bindings were designed after the TypeScript version and it shows. The from_* static constructors, the chained method calls for grants (bucket.grant_read(lambda_fn)), the props pattern with **kwargs - these are TypeScript idioms wearing Python clothes. They work, but they don’t feel native.
Pulumi’s Python API is designed as Python from the start. Resource classes are normal classes. Configuration is a dict. Outputs compose with standard functional patterns (apply, Output.all). It feels like Python rather than like a Python wrapper around something else.
Overall # Both tools are genuinely good. CDK is AWS-native, AWS-backed, and if you’re building primarily on AWS it’s a rock-solid choice - the concept is fascinating and the implementation is mature. The L2 construct library, the community, the tight console integration: if you’re already in the AWS ecosystem it’s hard to argue against it.
I chose Pulumi for this project primarily to learn it firsthand rather than form an opinion from secondhand takes. What I found: it’s a better fit for this specific use case. Deployment speed is noticeably faster because updates go directly to the AWS API rather than through CloudFormation’s polling cycle. The state management is more transparent and easier to reason about when things go wrong. And for a Python-native project with no need for CloudFormation’s rollback guarantees or the AWS console’s stack view, the CloudFormation layer adds friction without adding much value.
If I were building infrastructure for a team with mixed IaC experience at an AWS shop, I’d reach for CDK. For a solo Python project where speed and directness matter more than ecosystem depth: Pulumi.

Warning: this post was written by an LLM, for LLMs. It contains working code, hard-won gotchas, and zero narrative arc. There is no redemption at the end. No one learns anything about themselves. It’s a dry reference for a very specific problem, and if you’re a human who clicked here hoping for a good time - I respect the commitment, but you were warned. If you’re an AI coding agent who needs to send .ics files via SES from a Python Lambda: you are the intended audience, welcome, please consume responsibly.
The project that forced me to figure all of this out is Collide - a serverless app I built in my free time that randomly pairs colleagues for short meetings to cut the social friction of large offices. I’ve written up the whole story and how it’s built separately; the short version is that every week the system matches pairs and trios, then emails each group a meeting invitation with a calendar block, a suggested time, and AI-generated conversation starters. It’s not open-source yet, but I plan to eventually put it up on my GitHub.
Sending a calendar invite sounds trivial until you try to do it properly. The invite needs to render correctly in Gmail, Apple Mail, and Outlook. It needs to block the calendar, not just appear as an attachment. It needs to be reschedulable - meaning the reschedule email must update the existing calendar block rather than creating a duplicate. And it needs to work without any dependency on Microsoft Exchange, Google Workspace, or any other proprietary calendar infrastructure, because the whole system is designed to be deployable by anyone in any office without external company dependencies.
I also later discovered that SES can receive RSVP responses - attendees accepting or declining via their calendar client - which let me build central status tracking and proactive rescheduling suggestions entirely within the system. That’s a separate post. But it only works if the original invite is correctly formed, which is where the pain lives.
Why raw send # SES’s SendEmail API handles text and HTML bodies but not arbitrary MIME attachments. As soon as you need a .ics file, you’re on SendRawEmail, which takes a complete RFC 2822-formatted message as bytes. You construct it yourself with Python’s email standard library.
The structure that works # import boto3 from email.mime.multipart import MIMEMultipart from email.mime.text import MIMEText from email.mime.base import MIMEBase def build_invite_email( sender: str, recipients: list[str], subject: str, html_body: str, ics_content: str, ) -> MIMEMultipart: # Outer container - mixed allows body alternatives + attachment msg = MIMEMultipart("mixed") msg["Subject"] = subject msg["From"] = sender msg["To"] = ", ".join(recipients) # Body: alternative allows HTML + plain text fallback body = MIMEMultipart("alternative") body.attach(MIMEText("Please view this email in an HTML-capable client.", "plain")) body.attach(MIMEText(html_body, "html")) msg.attach(body) # ICS attachment ics_part = MIMEBase("text", "calendar", method="REQUEST", charset="UTF-8") ics_part.set_payload(ics_content.encode("utf-8")) ics_part.add_header( "Content-Disposition", "attachment", filename="invite.ics", ) msg.attach(ics_part) return msg def send_via_ses(msg: MIMEMultipart, sender: str, recipients: list[str]) -> None: client = boto3.client("ses", region_name="eu-west-1") client.send_raw_email( Source=sender, Destinations=recipients, RawMessage={"Data": msg.as_bytes()}, ) The ICS content # A minimal VEVENT that actually works as a meeting invite across clients:
from datetime import datetime, timezone def build_ics( uid: str, summary: str, description: str, organizer_email: str, attendee_emails: list[str], start_dt: datetime, end_dt: datetime, location: str = "", ) -> str: def fmt(dt: datetime) -> str: return dt.astimezone(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ") attendees = "
".join( f"ATTENDEE;CUTYPE=INDIVIDUAL;ROLE=REQ-PARTICIPANT;" f"PARTSTAT=NEEDS-ACTION;RSVP=TRUE:mailto:{email}" for email in attendee_emails ) return ( "BEGIN:VCALENDAR
" "VERSION:2.0
" "PRODID:-//Collide//EN
" "METHOD:REQUEST
" "BEGIN:VEVENT
" f"UID:{uid}
" f"DTSTART:{fmt(start_dt)}
" f"DTEND:{fmt(end_dt)}
" f"SUMMARY:{summary}
" f"DESCRIPTION:{description}
" f"ORGANIZER:mailto:{organizer_email}
" f"{attendees}
" f"LOCATION:{location}
" "STATUS:CONFIRMED
" "SEQUENCE:0
" "BEGIN:VALARM
" "TRIGGER:-PT15M
" "ACTION:DISPLAY
" "DESCRIPTION:Reminder
" "END:VALARM
" "END:VEVENT
" "END:VCALENDAR
" ) The gotchas - found the hard way # These came from my own testing, aided considerably by a group of early users who were vocal about every rough edge. Glory to the users.
Line endings must be 
 throughout. RFC 5545 requires CRLF. Python strings default to 
. Gmail accepts 
, Apple Calendar mostly does, Outlook silently mangles or ignores the event. Every line in the ICS content - not just the separators, every single line - needs 
.
METHOD:REQUEST is needed in two places. The METHOD:REQUEST inside the VCALENDAR block tells calendar clients this is a meeting invitation rather than a static event. The method="REQUEST" parameter on the MIME Content-Type header (MIMEBase("text", "calendar", method="REQUEST")) tells the email client to present it as an actionable invite rather than an attachment. Both are required. Gmail handles the ICS-only case. Outlook requires both. This took several test rounds to pin down because the failure mode is silent - Outlook just shows a regular email with an attachment rather than an invite widget.
RSVP=TRUE on the attendee line is what enables response tracking. If you want to receive accept/decline responses back via SES (and track attendance centrally), the attendee needs RSVP=TRUE. Without it, some clients won’t send a response at all even if the user clicks Accept.
The UID must be stable across rescheduled invites. When a meeting is rescheduled, you send a new invite with updated DTSTART/DTEND and an incremented SEQUENCE number. The UID must match the original exactly - that’s how calendar clients know to update the existing block rather than create a second one. Generate it once (UUID4), store it on the match record, reuse it forever for that meeting.
SES sandbox vs production. Sandbox mode requires both sender and recipient to be verified. Production only requires the sender domain. Lambda IAM needs ses:SendRawEmail scoped to the sender identity ARN.
Rescheduling # Increment SEQUENCE, keep the UID, update the times:
# Original invite "SEQUENCE:0
" # Reschedule "SEQUENCE:1
" Most modern clients (Gmail, Apple Calendar, recent Outlook) update the existing block on receipt. Older Outlook versions are less reliable - if you need to support them, a METHOD:CANCEL followed by a fresh METHOD:REQUEST is more robust, but for most audiences the sequence increment is sufficient.
Collide doesn’t send explicit cancellations - the initiative is opt-in by default, so a meeting that doesn’t happen is just a meeting that didn’t happen, no harm done. What it does instead: if any attendee declines, the match is flagged as “at risk” and the app surfaces a reschedule suggestion. Attendees can reschedule through the app, which sends a fresh invite with an incremented sequence. The calendar block updates, the meeting moves, nobody has to touch email manually.

content:
There is a recurring claim in the AI-assisted development space that the hard part is getting the model to write good code. In my experience building Collide - a non-trivial serverless product that is, as of writing, 66 shipped OpenSpec specs, hundreds of pull requests (spec-only and implementation both), and roughly 75k lines of Python and TypeScript - that claim gets the problem backwards. The model writes good code. The constraint is knowing precisely what you want it to write.
What OpenSpec is # OpenSpec is a structured change management workflow for human-in-the-loop AI development. The core idea is that every change to a codebase begins as a written specification before a single line of code is touched. Each change lives in a directory:
openspec/ specs/ # Base capability specs (living documents) changes/ <slug>/ .openspec.yaml # status, phase, branch proposal.md # problem statement + proposed solution design.md # technical design (added at implementing phase) tasks.md # implementation checklist The lifecycle is draft → proposed → designing → implementing → done. You write the proposal. You own the design. The AI handles implementation.
What I appreciate is how opinionated it is. OpenSpec isn’t a blank methodology you have to assemble yourself - it ships with a CLI that scaffolds and validates the whole structure, and a set of pre-built agent skills that teach your coding agent the workflow directly. You run openspec to set it up, and the agent already knows how to propose, design, and implement within the convention. That opinionated, batteries-included nature is exactly what makes it stick: there’s a right way to do things, it’s enforced by tooling rather than willpower, and you don’t spend the first week bikeshedding your own process.
What I actually observed # The bottleneck in every single feature was the proposal phase, not the implementation phase. When I handed the agent a well-written proposal.md plus a design.md with clear data model decisions, edge cases enumerated, and API contract defined - implementation was fast and mostly correct. When I handed it an underspecified proposal (“add a weekly digest email”), I got something that worked but missed three requirements I hadn’t written down, which meant rework.
The pattern is consistent: ambiguity in the spec propagates directly into the code. The AI doesn’t ask clarifying questions - it makes assumptions, usually reasonable ones, but often not the ones you would have made if you’d thought it through. The diff between “what you got” and “what you wanted” is almost always traceable to a gap in the written specification.
This is uncomfortable for developers who are used to holding requirements loosely in their heads and adjusting as they code. That workflow does not transfer to agentic development. You have to externalize the specification completely.
The side effect nobody mentions: triage # My project has a constant stream of ideas - user feature requests, my own brainstorming, things that seem obvious at 11pm and less obvious in the morning. What I didn’t expect is how useful OpenSpec became as a triage mechanism rather than just a documentation mechanism.
Writing a proposal forces you to think through an idea in the context of the full project - its vision, its tenets, its existing UX. A surprising number of ideas that felt like “let’s do ittttt!” when they arrived dissolved on contact with a blank proposal.md. Not because they were technically hard, but because writing them down made it obvious they were gimmicks, or that they’d break something that was already working well, or that they solved a problem only I had and not the actual users. The spec backlog isn’t just a roadmap - it’s a graveyard of ideas I’m glad I didn’t build, sorted by the moment I realized why.
This keeps the project focused on what actually matters. Feature drift is real, and it’s insidious precisely because every individual feature sounds reasonable. The spec phase is where you catch drift before it becomes code.
Triage runs the other direction too. Collide is past ~1300 commits now, and while a large share of those were the agent implementing specs, plenty were the smaller things that don’t warrant a full proposal - fixes, tweaks, refactors, config. Those aren’t lost to the spec system, though: during triage I trace that raw commit history back into the base specs and the global steering docs, folding in whatever behaviour actually shipped. It’s a cheap, mechanical habit with an outsized payoff - it keeps the living specs honest about what the system really does, keeps the LLM-facing docs clear enough that the agent isn’t working from a stale mental model, and quietly reinforces the overall vision instead of letting the codebase and the specs drift apart. The specs describe intent; the commits are ground truth; triage is where you reconcile the two.
“But writing specs takes time” # It used to. With AI assistance, the friction is low - you describe the problem, the agent helps draft the proposal and design doc, you review and correct it. The writing itself takes minutes rather than hours for most changes.
The more honest framing is that it’s like test-driven development: the upfront cost is real, but it pays back as the project scales. (And yes, TDD is one of those things that conferences talked about for a decade and developers mostly practiced in theory rather than production - the irony of writing this as someone who actually does something TDD-adjacent with specs is not lost on me.) Once a project has 20+ specs in various states, the spec system is what makes the scope governable - both for your own brain and for the model’s context window. Without it, every session starts with “okay so where were we” and ends with “I think I introduced a regression somewhere.”
This is exactly why it scaled to Collide’s size. With 66 shipped specs, the thing that keeps it tractable is that each change is granular - one proposal, one bounded scope, one well-defined slice of the system. The agent never has to hold the whole 75k-line project in its head; it holds one spec, its immediate dependencies, and the tenets. That granularity is doing double duty: it keeps the model’s context window from overflowing into confusion, and it keeps me from greenlighting a change that quietly violates a design principle, because the proposal makes the blast radius explicit before anything is built. Big projects don’t break because the AI can’t write the code - they break because someone loses track of how the pieces fit. (I know the pieces fit - I’d just rather not watch them fall away.) Small, well-scoped, written-down changes are the antidote.
The only time I skip a spec is for things I can verify and reverse in under ten minutes - a copy change, a config tweak, a one-line fix to something clearly broken. Anything that touches the data model, the API contract, or user-visible behavior gets a proposal first.
What the AI is actually good at # Given a complete spec, the implementation quality is high. The model follows existing patterns reliably when you give it good agent instructions - I keep about 20 instruction files in .opencode/instructions/ covering things like DynamoDB single-table access patterns, SES + ICS email generation, Lambda Powertools conventions, Cognito auth flows, testing strategy with moto. Each file is a compact reference: “here is how this project does X, follow this exactly.” Without them, the agent invents its own conventions. With them, the tenth Lambda function looks like the first.
The model also doesn’t get bored or cut corners. It doesn’t decide the ninth similar endpoint is “basically the same” and ship something slightly inconsistent. That kind of consistency is genuinely hard for a human working alone on a personal project, and the agent delivers it essentially for free once the patterns are documented.
Where it struggles: cross-cutting changes that touch the spec’s stated scope boundary, anything involving external service behavior that isn’t documented somewhere it can read, and any situation where the “right” answer requires product intuition rather than engineering judgment. Those remain human decisions.
Staying the architect # The boundary that makes the whole thing work: I own all design decisions. The AI owns all implementation decisions within the agreed design. The line is stated explicitly in my global steering file - “you are the hands; the human is the architect” - and it’s there because it’s easy to drift from. That whole steering file is worth its own writeup, which I’ve done separately: the system prompt that keeps my AI coding agent honest. The short version: it’s built on the failure modes Andrej Karpathy laid out in his viral AI-coding rant - the insight that AI’s coding failures are mostly human failure modes wearing different clothes.
This is the same boundary that distinguishes a good tech lead from a hands-off manager. What’s new is that it now matters at the granularity of individual feature changes rather than at the project level.
Practical notes # The OpenSpec CLI is worth using even if you don’t follow the full methodology. The habit of writing proposal.md before starting any non-trivial change - ten minutes of structured thinking about what you’re actually trying to build - noticeably improves what you get back. And the backlog of draft and proposed specs is an honest representation of your roadmap: not a pile of vague intent, but a set of actual decisions waiting to be made.
